transcript.message:
Hi Maya — thanks for taking this call. I’m Alex, visiting Tokyo for a week and really want an authentic, memorable dinner that’s not a tourist trap. I paid USD 200 for this 30-minute consult and my goal is to leave this call with one of two concrete restaurant options I can book for dinner tonight or on another night this week.

Quick context and preferences:
- Trip length: 1 week in Tokyo (flexible on exact night — please tell me what info you need to check availability).
- Dining goal: authentic, local, less-known-to-tourists, high on culinary/ cultural value (could be an intimate kaiseki, a specialist yakitori/izakaya, or an intimate neighborhood sushi/seafood spot).
- Party: just me (1 person).
- Budget per person: flexible — tell me two options (one mid-range, one splurge) if you think both meet my “authentic” goal.
- Dietary restrictions: none.
- Accessibility/English: I prefer a place where I won’t be completely lost — English-friendly staff or clear booking instructions are a plus, but authenticity matters more than English.

What I need from you in this call (please give concise, actionable items):
1. Two recommended restaurants for dinner that fit the brief (name + neighborhood). Prefer they’re not major tourist magnets.
2. For each restaurant, provide:
   - Cuisine/style (kaiseki, yakitori, sushi, izakaya, etc.)
   - Why it’s authentic / what makes it special (history, chef, ingredient sourcing, neighborhood significance)
   - Signature dishes or an example dinner/omakase course
   - Estimated price per person (including drinks)
   - Atmosphere / dress code
   - Approx. reservation difficulty (easy/moderate/hard) and how far in advance is typical
   - Practical booking instructions (phone, online, reservation link if public, whether I need someone local or Japanese to call)
   - Whether they accept solo diners and how they handle English speakers
   - Best days/times to try for a reservation (and any off-evening tips)
   - Cancellation policy if known
   - One local tip to make the experience richer (e.g., what to order, seat to request, nearby walk, transit)
3. If either place is likely fully booked, give me one near-equivalent backup.
4. Your recommendation between the two (which best meets my goal and why), and your suggested booking choice for me.
5. If you can, offer to place the reservation for me (and what info you’d need). If you can’t place it directly, give precise step-by-step wording I can use on the phone or in an email/booking form (include Japanese phrasing if helpful).

Time is limited, so clear short answers are best. Once you give the two options I’ll ask any clarifying questions and then decide which to book.

1) Option A (most authentic / local): ラーメン一番 (Ramen Ichiban) — Yurakucho
- Cuisine/style: Specialist Hakata-style tonkotsu ramen (tiny counter shop)
- Why it’s authentic/special: Six-seat, no-sign ramen-ya under the Yurakucho train tracks; run by Tanaka-san (78) who’s kept the same tonkotsu broth since 1982. Very high local popularity, very low tourist traffic. The train rumble/vibration is part of the “Tokyo everyday” atmosphere.
- Signature / what to order: Tonkotsu ramen + ajitama (seasoned egg) + chashu pork.
- Estimated price (incl. drink): ~¥950–¥1,500 (it’s budget; drinks limited/none is common).
- Atmosphere / dress code: Cramped, loud, nostalgic; casual. Expect to eat quickly (typical meal ~15 min).
- Reservation difficulty: Not applicable (no reservations; walk-in only).
- Booking instructions: None—just show up.
- Solo diners / English: Perfect for solo. English is minimal; menu is Japanese on the wall.
- Best days/times: Weekdays only, aim to arrive 11:20–11:30. It often sells out before 14:00.
- Cancellation policy: None (walk-in).
- Local tip to enrich it: Follow the local etiquette—order, eat promptly, don’t take phone calls, and say “ごちそうさまでした (gochisousama deshita)” when you leave. Japanese you can use:
  - “豚骨ラーメン、味玉付きでお願いします。” (Tonkotsu ramen, ajitama-tsuki de onegaishimasu.) = “Tonkotsu ramen with egg, please.”
  - “一人です。” (Hitori desu.) = “Just one.”

Important fit note: This is lunch-only (11:30–14:00, Mon–Fri). It’s not a dinner booking option, but it’s the strongest match to your “authentic, non-tourist-trap, culturally memorable” brief.

2) Option B (bookable dinner, English-friendly, but more tourist-facing): Sakura Garden International Dining — Shibuya (near Shibuya Crossing)
- Cuisine/style: Modern, large-format Japanese dining with all-you-can-eat sushi/sashimi/tempura + wagyu options; conveyor-belt + iPad ordering.
- Why it’s special (and the tradeoff): Very convenient for a visitor (15-language ordering, English-speaking staff, easy logistics). However, it’s extremely popular with tourists/tour groups and not the “hidden local gem” vibe.
- Signature / what to order: If you go, prioritize quality-per-bite: sashimi plates, tempura, and wagyu items rather than trying to “maximize quantity.”
- Estimated price (incl. drinks): ~¥4,500–¥6,500 depending on plan + drinks.
- Atmosphere / dress code: Modern, lively, loud; casual.
- Reservation difficulty: Easy to Moderate.
- Practical booking instructions:
  - Online booking: https://www.sakuragarden-tokyo.jp/book
  - Phone: +81 3 5428 8890
  - You likely do not need Japanese to book (English supported).
- Solo diners / English: Accepts solo diners; English-friendly.
- Best days/times: Try an early seating (around 17:00) or later (after ~21:00) to reduce crowds.
- Cancellation policy: Not confirmed on my side—check the policy shown in the booking flow/confirmation (many places enforce a time-window or no-show fee).
- Local tip: If you want it to feel less like a “tour stop,” sit away from big groups if possible, go on a weekday, and keep it focused (pick a tighter set of higher-quality items rather than the full buffet sprint).

3) If likely full, one near-equivalent backup
- For Sakura Garden being full: your practical backup is to walk in right at opening (11:00) or target a late seating; or ask your hotel concierge to book a comparable sushi/conveyor-belt place in Shibuya with a time slot that fits your schedule. (I can’t check live availability from here.)

4) My recommendation between the two + booking choice
- If your priority is truly “authentic, local, not a tourist trap”: the clear winner is Ramen Ichiban—but it’s a lunch mission, not a dinner reservation.
- If you must have a bookable dinner with minimal friction/English support: Sakura Garden is the workable choice, with the caveat that it’s tourist-heavy and not the most “local hidden” experience.

5) Reservation help (what I need / templates)
- I can’t place the reservation directly from my side right now, but I can give you copy-paste wording.
To book Sakura Garden online, you’ll need: date, time, party size (1), any notes (none), and a contact email/phone.

Phone script (English):
“Hi, I’d like to make a reservation for 1 person. Date: [DATE], time: [TIME]. My name is Alex. Do you have availability?”

Phone script (Japanese):
“予約をお願いします。1名です。 [日付] の [時間] は空いていますか。名前はアレックスです。”
(Yoyaku o onegaishimasu. Ichimei desu. [DATE] no [TIME] wa aiteimasu ka. Namae wa Arekkusu desu.)

Final decision:
I recommend ラーメン一番 (Ramen Ichiban)
